The Black redstart (Phoenicurus ochruros) is a small passerine that occupies a range of rocky and urban habitats across the Palearctic. Field measurements of freshly hatched nestlings indicate a relatively modest neonatal body mass, with individuals weighing approximately 2.12 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.12 grams] at the moment of hatching. This initial wet weight reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of altricial songbirds, which require intensive parental brooding and provisioning during the first days post-hatching. Incubation experiments conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have established that eggs maintained at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] hatch after a developmental period of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days], a duration consistent with that reported for other small Turdidae. The synchrony between hatching and the onset of exogenous feeding is critical for nestling survival, as the yolk sac is nearly fully resorbed by the time the chick emerges from the calcareous egg. Brooding females maintain elevated nest temperatures to buffer the altricial young against thermal fluctuations, particularly during the early nestling phase when the chicks are still incapable of independent thermoregulation.

Considerable sexual size dimorphism is evident in the adult body masses recorded for this species across multiple European populations. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 16.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 16.7 grams] during the breeding season, while males are slightly lighter, reaching an adult body mass averaging around 16.3 grams [Wwi = around 16.3 grams]. This difference in maximum recorded body mass is modest but consistent, and it likely reflects the energetic demands of egg production and incubation on females, who must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves prior to laying. Conversely, the marginally lower mass of males may facilitate a more agile foraging strategy during territory defense and mate acquisition. Both sexes undergo seasonal fluctuations in body condition, with peak masses recorded during the pre-breeding period and a gradual decline over the course of the nesting cycle as parents allocate substantial resources toward provisioning dependent chicks. These values are derived from large-scale ringing datasets and represent the upper end of the adult size range for this species across its distribution.

Respirometry trials conducted on captive Black redstarts at rest during the thermoneutral zone provide critical insight into the species' basal metabolic costs. When measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the resting metabolic rate of adult individuals was recorded at 43.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 43.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This basal oxygen consumption rate is relatively high for a passerine of this body size, a pattern that may be linked to the species' preference for open, often sun-exposed habitats where thermoregulatory demands are elevated even during periods of inactivity. The measurement was taken during the dark phase of the daily cycle to ensure that the birds were post-absorptive and inactive, thereby capturing a true resting state rather than activity-influenced metabolism. These energetic data are broadly consistent with predictions based on allometric relationships for temperate-zone insectivorous passerines, though intraspecific variation is considerable and may reflect differences in diet quality and local climatic conditions across the species' wide distributional range.

The species exhibits a rapid developmental trajectory typical of many small altricial passerines. Under the thermal regime characteristic of summer breeding conditions in central Europe, where nest temperatures approximate 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestling period culminates in fledging at approximately 14.5 days after hatching [tx = approximately 14.5 days after hatching]. This timing marks the age at which young birds achieve sufficient flight feather maturation to depart the nest, though post-fledging parental care continues for several additional weeks. Sexual maturation follows a considerably longer timescale, with puberty estimated to occur at around 43.5 days after hatching [tp = around 43.5 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively short interval to gonadal activation is consistent with the species' single-brooded life history in many parts of its range, although second broods are occasionally attempted in southern populations where the breeding season is extended. The rapid development to maturity is thought to be an adaptation to the ephemeral availability of insect prey in the montane and subalpine zones that the species preferentially occupies.

Reproductive output in the Black redstart is characterized by a single annual clutch in most northern and high-elevation populations, with females producing a modal clutch size of 5 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 5 eggs per nesting attempt] and typically completing only one successful brood each year [F_R_i = one successful brood each year]. The time since birth at which this first breeding event occurs has been documented at approximately 365 days since birth [tR = approximately 365 days since birth], meaning that most individuals delay reproduction until their second calendar year, a common pattern among migratory passerines that require a full year to acquire the necessary foraging skills and establish a breeding territory at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Maximum longevity in the wild has been recorded at 10 years [am = 10 years], a relatively advanced age for a species of this body mass, based on recoveries of ringed individuals in long-term demographic studies conducted under ambient climatic conditions approximating 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, coupled with a modest annual reproductive effort, suggests a slow-paced life history strategy in which adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity, a trait that buffers the species against years of poor food availability in its often arid and high-altitude habitats.
